title: Sävelten voima ja sitkeys
summary: This edited volume explores, through a selection of case studies, the ways in which music and politics have been historically intertwined. Music has often been closely connected to social transformations, political struggles, wars, and political violence, but also to peaceful processes of change. Music has served as an instrument of power, existed under the constraints of censorship and hegemonies, and given musical expression to people’s hopes and aspirations, including the pursuit of freedom, justice, and equality. Through music, people have expressed their values, emotions, identities, and political commitments. The volume is based on the idea of music as a historical and social force that can both challenge and sustain power and prevailing values. On the one hand, music has functioned as a transnational force for change in times of major transformations and revolutions. On the other hand, it has been used to stabilize social orders and maintain hegemonies and dominant ideologies. Music has had both concrete and symbolic significance in, for example, civil rights movements, the aspirations of nations and states seeking independence, and questions of peace. Music has fostered hope for the future and advanced new ideas and perspectives. Sounds of Power and Resilience approaches music, history, and politics together, through phenomena in which the power of music becomes visible in musical production and use as well as in reception and meaning. The editors and contributors also ask how music itself can function as an arena for political action and social interaction. Historical research on the social and political significance of music is interdisciplinary, drawing on diverse approaches, methods, and paradigms, as well as concepts and methods from fields such as history, sociology, anthropology, ethnology, psychology, and linguistics. The volume considers the challenges and possibilities involved in bringing these fields together and asks whether an interdisciplinary approach can help us identify something new about the connections between music, history, and politics. At the same time, it explores what interaction between disciplines can mean at the level of research and seeks to promote such dialogue. Historical research on music and musical life in the past seeks to understand and interpret its subject within its context, that is, within human communities. This volume also keeps in view the question of how, and on what grounds, the political character of that context is defined.
